title: Thermodynamic characterization of message-passing: Framework and initial study
authors: Kalana G. Abeywardena, Stark C. Draper
abstract: We study the thermodynamic efficiency of message-passing decoders using the mismatch cost framework. This framework quantifies the excess entropy generated when a system operates away from the thermodynamically optimal initial distribution. It provides a computable lower bound on irrecoverable energy loss. The decoder is modeled as a main decoding program with local message updates implemented as subroutines. Memory is treated as an external copying subsystem whose thermodynamic cost is excluded. Studying the $[7,4]$ Hamming code transmitted over a binary erasure channel, we show how the channel-induced initialization statistics and the step-wise evolution of the algorithmic state distribution during decoding determine the total mismatch cost. We further show that different thermodynamically optimal state distributions, representing different underlying physical implementations of the decoder, can produce different thermodynamic costs for identical decoding dynamics. Conditioning the input distribution on correctable and non-correctable erasure patterns further reveals distinct thermodynamic signatures. These results demonstrate that thermodynamic cost is jointly governed by decoding dynamics, input statistics, and hardware characteristics. This points to opportunities for thermodynamically-informed decoder design to realize energy-efficient physical implementations.
summary: This paper develops a thermodynamic framework using the mismatch cost to quantify the minimum energy loss associated with message-passing decoders. By analyzing the Hamming code, the authors demonstrate that the efficiency cost depends critically on not only the decoding algorithm but also on the statistical nature of the input data and the assumed hardware implementation. This suggests a path toward designing energy-efficient physical realizations of error-correcting codes.
main_problem: To thermodynamically characterize message-passing decoders by establishing a computable lower bound on the entropy production (mismatch cost) associated with irreversible decoding dynamics.
main_result: The thermodynamic cost of decoding is jointly governed by the decoding dynamics, the statistical structure of the input data, and the underlying hardware characteristics.
method: The study employs the mismatch cost framework, which quantifies excess entropy generated when the system deviates from the thermodynamically optimal initial distribution.
model_or_system: The model is a message-passing decoder, initially studied using the [7, 4] Hamming code transmitted over a binary erasure channel (BEC). It is treated as a finite-state system evolving over time.
key_observables: Mismatch Cost, Entropy Production ($\Theta_{EP}$), Algorithmic State Distribution, and Thermodynamic Cost.
important_parameters: Erasure probability ($\epsilon$), the structure of input patterns (correctable vs. non-correctable), and the choice of thermodynamically optimal prior distribution.
main_assumptions: The analysis abstracts away from detailed physical/circuit-level dynamics, focusing on the algorithmic state evolution, and assumes the mismatch cost provides a valid lower bound on entropy production.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mismatch cost for inputs restricted to correctable ($\mathcal{X}_D^{EE}$) versus non-correctable ($\mathcal{X}_D^{EH}$) erasure patterns, showing cost dependence on the erasure probability $\epsilon$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the thermodynamic framework using the mismatch cost, applies it to the Hamming code over a BEC, and then analyzes how input statistics (correctable vs. non-correctable erasures) critically influence the resulting thermodynamic cost.
why_interesting: While focused on classical coding theory, the rigorous application of non-equilibrium thermodynamics (entropy production, lower bounds) to an algorithmic process provides a powerful, general methodology for analyzing energy dissipation in complex computational systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems.
